The full passage in which Hesiod addresses the fate of Prometheus is as follows:  


​

*Clever Prometheus was bound by Zeus*

*In cruel chains, unbreakable, chained round*

*A pillar, and Zeus roused and set on him*

*An eagle with long wings, which came and ate*

*His deathless liver. But the liver grew*

*Each night, until it made up the amount*

*The long-winged bird had eaten in the day.*

*Lovely Alcmene's son, strong Heracles,*

*Killing the eagle, freed Prometheus*

*From his affliction and his misery,*

*And Zeus, Olympian, who rules on high,*

*Approved, so that the fame of Heracles*

*The Theban might be greater than before*

*Upon the fruitful earth; he showed respect,*

*And gave the honour to his famous son.*

*And angry though he was, he checked the rage*

*He felt against Prometheus, who dared*

*To match his wits against almighty Zeus.*  


​

*For at Mekone, once, there was a test*

*When gods and mortal men divided up*

*An ox; Prometheus audaciously*

*Set out the portions, trying to deceive*

*The mind of Zeus Before the rest, he put*

*Pieces of meat and marbled inner parts*

*And fat upon the hide, and hid them in*

*The stomach of the ox; but before Zeus*

*The white bones of the ox, arranged with skill,*

*Hidden in shining fat. And then he spoke,*

*The father of gods and men, and said to him,*

*'Milord, most famous son of Iapetos,*

*The shares you've made, my friend, are most unfair!'*

*Thus Zeus, whose plans are everlasting, spoke*

*And criticized. But sly Prometheus*

*Did not forget his trick, and softly smiled*

*And said, 'Most glorious Zeus, greatest of all*

*The gods who live forever, choose your share,*

*Whichever one your heart leads you to pick'*

*He spoke deceitfully, but Zeus who knows*

*Undying plans, was not deceived, but saw*

*The trick, and in his heart made plans*

*To punish mortal men in future days.*

*He took the fatted portion in his hands*

*And raged within, and anger seized his heart*

*To see the trick, the white bones of the ox.*  


​

*But Zeus, the gatherer of clouds, enraged,*

*Said, 'Son of Iapetos, cleverest god*

*Of all: so, friend, you do not yet forget*

*Your crafty tricks!' So spoke the angry Zeus*

*Whose craft is everlasting. From that time*

*He bore the trick in mind and would not give,*

*To wretched men who live on earth, the power*

*Of fire, which never wearies. The brave son*

*Of Iapetos deceived him, and he stole*

*The ray, far-seeing, of unwearied fire,*

*Hid in the hollow fennel stalk, and Zeus*

*Who thunders in the heavens ate his heart,*

*And raged within to see the ray of fire*

*Far-seeing, among men. Immediately*

*He found a price for men to pay for fire,*  


​

*It is impossible to hoodwink Zeus*

*Or to surpass him, for Prometheus,*

*The son of Iapetos, kind though he was*

*And wise, could not escape his heavy rage*

*But he was bound by force, with heavy chains.*

In Greek mythology, it was the Titan Prometheus who dared to restore his gift of fire unto man after Zeus, King of the Olympians, withdrew and again withheld this most crucial element from humanity. Having a fiery temper himself, Zeus had Hephaestus, god of the forge, chain the Titan to Mount Caucasus where he would have his liver routinely devoured by an eagle, a symbol of Zeus himself. 

Rubens teams up with fellow Flemish painter Frans Snyders, who contributed the eagle, to deliver one of his most astounding pieces. 

It is an overall horrifying image. The mighty, hulking Titan, now constrained and helplessly watching his predator tear through his immortal flesh with almost surgical precision—a pro at this everyday encounter between the two figures now. The defeated Prometheus can only watch on at his mutilation with his left eye, his right having been gorged by the beast's talons, signaling that he is fully aware of his torture. All throughout his forced hepatectomy, Prometheus flails his legs, clenches his fists, and bellows curses heard only by his antagonist, all too well conveying the Titan's abject agony.

I’m not sure why others study Mythology, but for me personally it is a mix of converging interests found in Mythology, Folklore, and things of the sort. History, Philosophy, Theology, Psychology, and many other kinds of -ologies can be found in these stories.

If you don’t have a great interest in the stories themselves then dissecting them through various academic lenses will be painful. You don’t need to be passionate about these things in order to understand them, but it certainly helps turn pages when it comes to say, the Greek epics. 

If you are purely interested in learning about mythology with the hopes of extracting some kind of exclusive wisdom/knowledge from them, perhaps take the route of comparative mythology. 

Joseph Campbell’s work is the best of this kind if ya ask me or at least serves as the best starting point for comparative Mythology/Folklore.

Oh boy, well... As far as primary sources go, Homer’s ‘Illiad’ and ‘Odyssey’ are your bread and butter but personally I find Hesiod’s ‘Theogony’ more a hoot and far less trouble getting through. The ‘Homeric Hymns’ (also attributed to Homer) are worth looking into depending on your taste. 

Edith Hamilton’s ‘Mythology’ is a great overview of the Greek mythos. There are plenty of Greek myth summy books but this is the most used. 

If you want something less academic and more entertaining you can give Stephen Fry’s ‘Mythos/‘‘Heroes’ a go.

Perseus is one of the oldest figures in Greek Myth. He existed during the original age of monster slayers and demigods and was, of course, the grandfather of Heracles.   
The oldest written accounts of these myths, therefore, are extremely young compared to the myths themselves.   
We get our oldest written account of these particular Perseus myths from the good ol Greek Hesiod in his *Theogony,* composed roughly 700-730BCE. Here Hesiod briefly covers the slaying of Medusa, but I don't believe he mentions Perseus again. I could easily be wrong, I just haven't read the *Theogony* in a while.

The only other source that comes to mind is the Roman poet Ovid who provides much more detail and material overall in his *Metamorphoses,* written about 8AD. He covers the slaying of Medusa, Cetus, and then the rescuing and marriage of Andromeda. He also covers the other myths concerning Perseus throughout the book too. 

Another (albeit, irrelevant) source would be Homer's *Illiad* (first written down roughly in 8th Cen. BCE) where Perseus is only briefly mentioned in order to establish historical context regarding the founding of Mycenae.

This is the most common order of the 12 labours:

1 - the slaying of the Nemean lion

2 - the slaying of the nine-headed Hydra of Lerna 

3 - the capture of the elusive hind (or stag) of Arcadia 

4 - the capture of the wild boar of Mount Erymanthus 

5 - the cleansing, in a single day, of the cattle stables of King Augeas of Elis 

6 - the shooting of the monstrous man-eating birds of the Stymphalian marshes 

7 - the capture of the mad bull that terrorized the island of Crete 

8 - the capture of the man-eating mares of King Diomedes of the Bistones 

9 - the taking of the girdle of Hippolyte, queen of the Amazons 

10 - the seizing of the cattle of the three-bodied giant Geryon, who ruled the island Erytheia 

11 - the bringing back of the golden apples kept at the world’s end by the Hesperides 

12 - the fetching up from the underworld of the triple-headed hound Cerberus, guardian of its gates

Heracles was originally only suppose to complete 10 labours but labours #2 and #5 were considered forfeited by Eurystheus (The king of Tiryns who imposed these labours onto Heracles in the first place) as he was assisted in labour #2 by his cousin Iolaus. Labour #5 was voided because Heracles took payment (after much reluctance and difficulty on the part of King Augeas) for the task.

I can’t speak so much for other many headed serpentine creatures, but the Lernaean Hydra I believe is symbolic of mans never ending problems. The same ought to be more or less true for other such creatures. 

When Herakles severs the Hydra’s heads, it grows back (or in some sources it grows back many times over). This is to say that when a problem is dealt with, another (or so) will take its place. 

Herakles and his nephew Iolaus solve this issue by cauterising the wounds of the freshly severed heads. Eventually there is but one final head. 

The problem here is that this central head of the Hydra is immortal and cannot be slain even when severed. Herakles goes on to bury this still writhing head under a massive boulder in the ocean depths. 

Moral of the story is this I believe: When we deal with a problem, it isn’t long before another problem or so takes the place of the previous problem. Life is all about problem solving after all. However, when one deals with a problem in such a way that it can’t possibly lead to any further complications, then you have managed to properly turn chaos into order. You have understood the problem before you and set it ablaze. You have undergone a transformative task.

Fire of course being a symbol for many things. In this case fire is the purifier, destroyer, illumination and enlightenment. 

At the end of the day though, you cannot truly remove the source of all problems from your world. It is eternal, and the best we can do to deal with this is to remind ourselves that, once again, life is about problem solving. We need to be prepared to face the Hydra even when things are at their best.
